title: Local Legend Blamed A Giant For This. Geology Explains It Instead.
description:
Forty thousand stone columns line the coast of Northern Ireland, packed together so perfectly that legend says a giant built them. The real explanation is volcanic -- and it has a genuine twist connecting it to Scotland.

scenes.text: Along the coast of Northern Ireland, there are forty thousand stone columns, packed together so perfectly it looks like someone built them on purpose.
Local legend says an Irish giant named Finn McCool built it himself, as a bridge to fight a Scottish giant across the sea.

When the Scottish giant actually showed up, Finn's wife disguised him as a giant baby. The Scottish giant took one look, assumed the father must be enormous, and fled back across the water -- tearing up the bridge behind him.

The real explanation is volcanic. Around fifty to sixty million years ago, molten lava cooled and cracked here, and the exact way it contracted as it cooled is what formed these uniform, mostly six-sided columns.
The tallest columns stand about twelve meters high, and in places the solidified lava bed underneath them is twenty eight meters thick.
There's a genuine twist to the legend, too. Across the water in Scotland, Fingal's Cave has the exact same kind of basalt columns -- because both were actually formed by the same ancient lava flow.
Which do you find more interesting -- the real geology, or the giant's legend it inspired?
